hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks and America 250 events
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4.
hero.body:
North Palm Beach residents and visitors will gather at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4 for a full day of family-friendly activities, entertainment and fireworks. The free community event recognizes America's 250th anniversary this year, adding special significance to the annual holiday celebration in Palm Beach County. The festivities conclude with a fireworks display scheduled for 9 p.m.

The celebration kicks off with a community pool party beginning at 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Attendees can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. Event organizers say the pool deck and lawn areas will serve as a festive backdrop for activities throughout the day.

Starting at 4:30 p.m., families can participate in lawn games and activities such as cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga and face painting. Live music from Solstice Reign is scheduled to begin around 6 p.m. The Clubhouse will host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet from 4:30 p.m., offering attendees dining options while they enjoy the entertainment and activities.

According to Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, the golf course provides one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display. The combination of activities, entertainment and dining options creates a full day of celebration for the community to enjoy together.

cards.headline: Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for state storm repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Martin County manufactured home owners will be able to apply for state funding to pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits starting in August, ac.
cards.body:
Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for state funding to pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits starting in August through a new online portal, according to Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services. Senate Bill 594, which took effect July 1st, opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding for mobile and manufactured home owners across Florida. About 75% of Martin County's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can either fill out an online application or call the Martin County Human Services office to have one mailed to them.

The law follows an investigation that found nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida, about two-thirds of the state's more than 1 million such homes, were built before today's federal safety standards and cannot withstand modern storms. The investigation was prompted by an EF-3 tornado that struck Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce, destroying 138 homes and killing six residents. Spanish Lakes resident Paula Richards received estimates costing $10,000 to $15,000 for storm-hardening work. The funding covers lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance. Stellatos said funding operates on a first come, first served basis. Visit the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website to check income eligibility and contact information for your county or city.

cards.headline: Florida begins enforcement of new terrorism designation law as DeSantis targets seven groups on day one
cards.body:
Florida moved quickly to implement a new state law that grants officials the power to designate organizations as terrorist groups. On Wednesday, Governor Ron DeSantis announced the first slate of targets at a Tampa press conference with FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass and Statewide Prosecutor Brad McVay, just hours after the statute took effect on July 1. The governor said the state is preparing to designate the Muslim Brotherhood, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), Antifa, cartel-linked groups including Tren de Aragua and Sinaloa-related organizations, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The law takes effect on July 1, today, and so we are not going to waste any time," DeSantis said.

HB 1471, officially titled "Systems of Law and Terrorist Organizations," authorizes Florida's Chief of Domestic Security to recommend designations for domestic or foreign terrorist groups. Those recommendations must then be approved or rejected by the governor and Florida Cabinet by majority vote before they take effect. Designated organizations can face public funding restrictions, possible corporate dissolution in certain circumstances, and penalties tied to material support. According to DeSantis, the designations would affect state and local funding, colleges and universities, and Florida's K-12 school choice scholarship program.

DeSantis presented Wednesday's announcement as a continuation and strengthening of a December executive order that targeted CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood. That earlier action was quickly challenged in federal court, and in March a judge temporarily blocked enforcement after CAIR, CAIR Florida, and civil rights groups sued, claiming it violated constitutional protections. DeSantis said the new law provides better legal footing for the state's efforts. "We did need to have more of a legal structure to be able to add teeth to these designations," he said. Glass echoed this sentiment, saying the law gives the state "more tools in the toolbox."

Attorneys representing CAIR signaled they expect another legal battle. Scott McCoy, deputy legal director of the Southern Poverty Law Center, stated that "regardless of what Gov. DeSantis calls it, the U.S. Constitution is supreme across our nation, including in Florida." He added that on CAIR's behalf, the Southern Poverty Law Center, American Civil Liberties Union, and other partners "look forward to responding in court." The designations remain unofficial until the Cabinet approves them. While no regular Cabinet meeting is scheduled for July, DeSantis indicated officials may convene in an emergency session to approve the designations.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach gets $2 million for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a long-discussed drainage project along Australian Avenue, a roadway that has flooded for decades.
cards.body:
The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for drainage improvements along Australian Avenue, a roadway that Palm Beach County leaders have identified as needing major upgrades. The project targets Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street. State Sen. Mack Bernard called securing the funding a major step forward after the governor vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The $2 million covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost.

Residents have described years of flooding from even routine rain. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, said he has been riding his bike through flooded streets since childhood. Marion Hawkins, who lives near the roadway, calls it "Lake Australian Avenue" because rainwater comes up to her driveway and yard, leaving debris scattered across her property. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented improvement plans three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to accommodate larger underground drainage pipes. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled through 2029.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County residents hit with thousands in retroactive sewer fees from Delray Beach
cards.body:
Homeowners in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood are facing unexpected bills for years of unpaid sewer fees from the city of Delray Beach, with some residents receiving notices totaling more than $4,000. Several homeowners along Franwood Drive received demands for back payments covering up to three years of charges, plus new monthly sewer fees going forward. Candace Etzler received a notice for $3,139, and at least a dozen other homeowners in the neighborhood received similar bills. Ruth Stephens said her total bill came to $4,494.92. The situation began in 1998 when nearby development disrupted the residents' septic systems, and state law required them to connect to the closest municipal sewer system. The city of Delray Beach completed an audit in April 2026, which triggered the retroactive billing.

The sudden bills caught residents off guard, and many are questioning how the charges were calculated. Stephens said the notices were shocking because they had attempted to pay previously but were told by the city they did not need to. Etzler challenged the calculation method, asking how the city arrived at the specific 36-month period at $90 per month. Both residents expressed concern about the financial burden of these unexpected expenses. Some homeowners have already paid the fees or enrolled in payment plans because they fear their sewer service could be disconnected if they do not settle the bills.

City Commissioner Juli Casale issued a statement defending the billing practices. She said when a sewer connection is identified, the city has a responsibility to determine what costs were incurred and recover the applicable fees. Casale explained that this approach ensures public utility costs are paid by those actually receiving the service rather than being shifted to taxpayers. The city maintains that the billing follows standard utility recovery procedures.

County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she has contacted the county attorney to examine the legality of the back charges and the monthly payments moving forward. The county attorney's office will investigate whether the city's retroactive billing and fee structure comply with applicable laws. For now, residents remain frustrated with the situation, hoping for answers and potential relief from the substantial bills they were not expecting to receive.

hero.headline: Wellington Green's vacant Nordstrom could become 620-unit apartment complex
hero.body:
Bainbridge Companies has submitted a proposal to transform the empty Nordstrom building at the Mall at Wellington Green into a major residential development. The plan calls for converting 18 acres into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex, with the existing structure to be demolished if approved. The development would feature a variety of unit sizes housed in three towers along with a parking structure.

Village Manager Jim Barnes explained that the project would offer multiple housing options for residents. "One-, two- and three-bedroom units including three towers and a parking structure," Barnes said. He emphasized that the development responds to a significant housing shortage affecting the region and beyond. "Not only in the county, but throughout the state, and even out of the state, there is a shortage of housing units," Barnes said.

Not all Wellington residents support the proposal. Richard Meyers, a decade-long resident, expressed opposition to adding more apartments to the area. "There's already a bunch of apartment complexes around the mall; I don't think we need more," Meyers said. Traffic concerns also emerged from some community members. Gaby Martinez worried that increased density would strain local roads and create commuting problems. "Even just adding daily commutes to that area seems like it might create some bottlenecks," Martinez said.

Village leadership has framed the project as potentially beneficial to the mall's long-term future. Barnes noted that additional development near the mall could support the remaining retailers, which continue to perform strongly. He pointed out that anchor stores including Macy's, Dillard's and JCPenney remain high-performing locations. Barnes specifically highlighted the success of the Macy's location at the mall, calling it "the highest-performing store in the state." The village has not yet announced a timeline or cost estimate for the project, and the plans remain subject to approval.

cards.headline: Palm Beach International Airport name change to Donald J. Trump International takes effect July 9
cards.teaser: Palm Beach International Airport is in the process of becoming Donald J. Trump International Airport, with the official name change set to take effect July 9.
cards.body:
Palm Beach International Airport's official name change to Donald J. Trump International Airport takes effect July 9. Signs are already being swapped out as part of a transition funded by the state of Florida at a cost of $2.75 million. The official three-letter designation will change from PBI to DJT, used for airline reservations and navigation purposes, with that transition expected to happen in August. The airport is still owned by Palm Beach County, but Trump owns the trademark on the new name. Airport officials said nothing should change for passengers beyond the signage.

Two lawsuits are attempting to stop the name change. George Poncy, a local pilot and one of the plaintiffs suing to block it, said the state seems to be stalling and delaying any hearing before a judge. The airport posted a statement on its website addressing the transition, saying it recognizes that the required name change may be received in different ways by passengers and expressed gratitude for their continued support through the transition period.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detention facility closed after one year of operation in Everglades
cards.teaser: One year after Florida opened the controversial Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility in the Everglades, ICE confirmed all detainees have been removed and the facility has closed.
cards.body:
Florida's Alligator Alcatraz detention facility in the Everglades closed after one year of operation on June 16, when ICE confirmed all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. President Donald Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis announced the facility's opening on July 1, 2025, marking the first time a state had run a detention facility exclusively for immigration detainees. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County and built the facility in eight days using emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management.

The facility drew immediate scrutiny from multiple fronts. Immigration attorneys raised alarms about conditions inside, while the ACLU filed a federal lawsuit over detainees' access to legal counsel. Friends of the Everglades, led by Director Eve Samples, joined the Miccosukee Tribe in filing a separate lawsuit claiming construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through Alligator Alcatraz, with most estimates putting the total cost at more than $1 billion. A $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers to cover costs. The ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits remain active.

cards.headline: Martin County clinic sees more patients after ACA subsidies expired
cards.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year, and the clinic says it has room for more.
cards.body:
Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of Volunteers in Medicine, said more than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. The expiration of the enhanced financial assistance program at the start of the year has left many people without health insurance and, in some cases, without access to medical care. Only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, but estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access. Bromberg said the clinic has capacity for more patients.

Rokaya McGarry is one patient who sought care after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired and she could no longer afford health insurance. She said she fell very ill after losing her mother and in a moment of desperation called the clinic, which took her in within a day. To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. The clinic provides free medical care with no strings attached.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after earthquakes in Venezuela
cards.teaser: Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira, collapsing buildings and killing members of her family.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife when earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week. Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, called De La Correa repeatedly in the middle of the night after the earthquake hit. De La Correa's parents survived, but the earthquakes destroyed their home and businesses. Her mother's children's clothing store was located inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely. Her uncle's apartment building also collapsed moments before he entered it.

Claudia, a volleyball player who had planned to study dentistry, was rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. De La Correa's uncle, a former Navy member, searched through the rubble in darkness after electricity knocked out across the area. When he found Claudia dead, he stayed behind to help rescue her trapped best friend, who was rescued after around 13 hours but was later killed when another section of the structure collapsed. Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign aiming to raise $15,000 to support De La Correa's relatives. De La Correa's parents return daily to the ruins searching for salvageable belongings and have recovered some clothing, photos and documents.

hero.headline: Benjamin Franklin artifact collection opening July 6 at Historical Society of Palm Beach County
hero.teaser: More than 120 pieces from one of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will be on display in downtown West Palm Beach to celebrate America's 250th birthday.
hero.body:
One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will be on display at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach starting July 6. Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens owns the collection with his brother, and they are displaying it to celebrate America's 250th birthday. The exhibit, titled Benjamin Franklin: Creating an American Icon, features more than 120 pieces spanning Franklin's life as a statesman, printer, and inventor.

The exhibition showcases over 50 books written by, printed by, or about Franklin, along with items from his printing business. "There's so much more to Franklin than just his years as a founding father," Jacobson said. Among the standout pieces is a grandfather clock originally from Franklin's home in Philadelphia, a plate inscribed "B. Franklin," and original medallions created when Franklin represented France during the American Revolution. The collection also includes artwork and an original portrait of the founding father. One of the most distinctive items is the glass armonica, which Franklin called his favorite invention. According to Jacobson, "You play it by wetting your fingers in a bowl, have the glass bowls spin and play it like a piano."

Jacobson's stepfather started collecting Franklin artifacts 50 years ago. Jacobson and his brother eventually purchased the remaining pieces of the collection and have continued adding to it for 15 years. "My brother and I have been collecting Franklin in tandem ever since," Jacobson said. Notable highlights include a copy of Experiments and Observations on Electricity Made at Philadelphia that was owned by Franklin's son William, a tall-case tidal clock that Franklin kept in his Philadelphia home, and a plaster model for the Libertas Americana medal, which Franklin designed and Augustin Dupre executed.

The exhibit is free and open to the public from July 6 through August at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County, located at 300 N Dixie Hwy. Jacobson hopes visitors will use these artifacts as a gateway to learn more about American history and the founding period. "Just anything you could ever imagine with Franklin's face on it, other than a $100 bill, will be here," Jacobson said, highlighting the comprehensiveness of the collection on display.

cards.headline: Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for state storm repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Martin County manufactured home owners will be able to apply for state funding to pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits starting in August, ac.
cards.body:
Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for state funding to pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits starting in August through a new online portal, according to Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services. Senate Bill 594, which took effect July 1st, opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding for mobile and manufactured home owners across Florida. About 75% of Martin County's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can either fill out an online application or call the Martin County Human Services office to have one mailed to them.

The law follows an investigation that found nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida, about two-thirds of the state's more than 1 million such homes, were built before today's federal safety standards and cannot withstand modern storms. The investigation was prompted by an EF-3 tornado that struck Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce, destroying 138 homes and killing six residents. Spanish Lakes resident Paula Richards received estimates costing $10,000 to $15,000 for storm-hardening work. The funding covers lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance. Stellatos said funding operates on a first come, first served basis. Visit the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website to check income eligibility and contact information for your county or city.

cards.headline: Vacant Nordstrom at Wellington Green could become 620-unit apartment complex
cards.teaser: Bainbridge Companies submitted plans to convert 18 acres of the empty Nordstrom store into a multifamily apartment complex with three towers and a parking structure.
cards.body:
Bainbridge Companies has submitted plans to convert 18 acres of the vacant Nordstrom at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex. The existing building would be demolished if the project is approved. Village Manager Jim Barnes said the development would include a mix of one-, two- and three-bedroom units along with three towers and a parking structure. Barnes indicated the project addresses a broader housing shortage affecting the county, state and beyond.

Some residents oppose the proposal. Richard Meyers, who has lived in Wellington for more than a decade, said there are already numerous apartment complexes around the mall and he does not believe more are needed. Gaby Martinez expressed concerns about traffic, noting that added density could strain local roads and create bottlenecks. Barnes suggested that new development near the mall could benefit existing retailers. He noted that Macy's, Dillard's and JCPenney continue to perform well, and stated that the Macy's at the Mall at Wellington Green is the highest-performing store in the state. No timeline or cost estimate has been announced, and the plans have not been approved.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz one year later: Facility closed after controversy, lawsuits and $1 billion cost
cards.teaser: The Everglades detention facility closed in June after one year of operations that drew legal challenges over detainee conditions and environmental violations.
cards.body:
One year after opening Alligator Alcatraz in the Everglades, Florida's controversial immigration detention facility has closed following legal challenges and mounting costs. President Donald Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis announced the facility's opening in July 2025, marking the first time a state ran a detention facility exclusively for immigration detainees. The state used emergency powers to commandeer a Miami-Dade County landing strip and emergency funding through the Florida Division of Emergency Management to construct the facility in eight days. Using ICE data, investigators found approximately 70 percent of detainees had no criminal record, contradicting government claims that only dangerous migrants would be housed there.

The facility faced immediate legal challenges from multiple fronts. The American Civil Liberties Union sued over detainees' access to legal counsel, citing restrictions on attorney visits and monitored phone calls. Friends of the Everglades, led by Director Eve Samples, joined the Miccosukee Tribe and environmental groups in a separate federal lawsuit claiming construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. Immigration attorney Eric Lee reported severe conditions inside the facility. A $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers responsible for costs exceeding $1 billion. ICE confirmed on June 16 that all detainees were removed ahead of hurricane season. DeSantis reported that 21,000 detainees were deported through the facility. Both lawsuits remain active.

cards.headline: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County sees more patients after ACA subsidies expired
cards.teaser: A free medical clinic in Martin County is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year and says it has room for more uninsured people.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, which serves low-income families in Martin County, is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year. The expiration of the enhanced financial assistance program has left many people without health insurance and, in some cases, without access to medical care. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of Volunteers in Medicine, said more than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year, a number he said is worrisome because many preventive screenings that can prevent serious health outcomes are being missed.

Rokaya McGarry is one patient who could no longer afford health insurance after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired. She said panic set in because she knew an emergency room was her only option for care. After falling very ill following the loss of her mother, McGarry called the clinic, which took over her care within a day. Bromberg said only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, but estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access. To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. The clinic provides free medical care with no strings attached.

cards.headline: Vero Beach nonprofit Latinas Nexus Network needs box truck to deliver Venezuela earthquake relief supplies
cards.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach has collected more than 100 boxes of supplies for Venezuela earthquake relief and needs a box truck by Thursday to transport them to Miami.
cards.body:
Latinas Nexus Network, a Vero Beach nonprofit, has collected more than 100 boxes of supplies for Venezuela earthquake relief and is partnering with Global Empowerment Mission in Miami to deliver them. Founder Lourana Navarro said the organization began collecting donations Friday afternoon in response to the 7.5-magnitude earthquake that struck Venezuela. Co-founder Juliana Marino said the community response exceeded expectations, with residents bringing donations that filled far more boxes than anticipated. The supplies range from diapers to medical supplies.

The volume of donations has created a logistical challenge. Marino explained that the organization initially planned to transport everything in their personal vehicles to Miami, but there is no longer room. Navarro is urgently asking the community to donate the use of a 12 to 16-foot box truck by Thursday so the supplies can be loaded and delivered to Global Empowerment Mission in Miami on Friday. For Navarro, the cause is personal: she was born in Venezuela and has family near the earthquake's epicenter. Anyone able to help can contact Navarro at 954-205-0700 or Marino at 772-913-0805.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman Carla Alvarado launches fundraiser for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes
cards.teaser: Carla Alvarado, who lives in West Palm Beach, launched a GoFundMe campaign after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira, killing members of her best friend's family.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week. Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, woke De La Correa with nonstop phone calls in the middle of the night after the earthquakes struck. De La Correa's parents survived, but several relatives did not, including her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, and her uncle and his wife.

The losses came just weeks after De La Correa returned from her first visit to Venezuela in several years, where she had announced that she and her partner are expecting a baby. The family gathered for Mother's Day during her final weekend in the country. Claudia, who had planned to study dentistry, was rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. The earthquakes also destroyed De La Correa's parents' home and businesses, including her mother's children's clothing store located in a shopping mall that collapsed entirely. Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign aiming to raise $15,000 to support De La Correa's relatives. De La Correa said the support from friends and strangers has become a lifeline as her parents return daily to the ruins of their apartment building searching for salvageable belongings.

cards.headline: Fourth of July celebrations across Treasure Coast mark America's 250th birthday with fireworks and festivals
cards.teaser: Communities across the Treasure Coast are pulling out all the stops to mark America's 250th birthday on Saturday with events ranging from sunrise 5Ks to drone shows and spectacular fireworks displays.

The evening Fabulous Finale runs from 6:30 to 9:30 p.m. at Countess de Hoernle Park, featuring live music and a 20-minute fireworks display at 9:10 p.m.

Delray Beach's annual Fourth of July Celebration, a family-friendly tradition for over 50 years, is expected to draw more than 20,000 people beginning at 5 p.m. on East Atlantic Avenue and A1A. The event includes a 1976 Bicentennial Time Capsule Opening at 5 p.m., a 60-foot Flag Raising with National Anthem at 6 p.m., and live music starting at 6:30 p.m., with fireworks at 9 p.m. All-day activities feature food trucks, vendors, arts and crafts, face painting, glitter tattoos, carnival games, a photo booth and toddler soft play.

hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks and America 250 events
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4.
hero.body:
North Palm Beach residents and visitors will gather at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4 for a full day of family-friendly activities, entertainment and fireworks. The free community event recognizes America's 250th anniversary this year, adding special significance to the annual holiday celebration in Palm Beach County. The festivities conclude with a fireworks display scheduled for 9 p.m.

The celebration kicks off with a community pool party beginning at 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Attendees can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. Event organizers say the pool deck and lawn areas will serve as a festive backdrop for activities throughout the day.

Starting at 4:30 p.m., families can participate in lawn games and activities such as cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga and face painting. Live music from Solstice Reign is scheduled to begin around 6 p.m. The Clubhouse will host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet from 4:30 p.m., offering attendees dining options while they enjoy the entertainment and activities.

cards.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting programs through September
cards.teaser: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season this summer.
cards.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season through September. The center said guests can participate in seasonal experiences including guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. The programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches.

The center's Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations during the programs may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment. Loggerhead Marinelife Center's education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups continue encouraging beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.headline: Florida begins enforcement of new terrorism designation law as DeSantis targets seven groups on day one
hero.body:
Florida moved quickly to implement a new state law that grants officials the power to designate organizations as terrorist groups. On Wednesday, Governor Ron DeSantis announced the first slate of targets at a Tampa press conference with FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass and Statewide Prosecutor Brad McVay, just hours after the statute took effect on July 1. The governor said the state is preparing to designate the Muslim Brotherhood, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), Antifa, cartel-linked groups including Tren de Aragua and Sinaloa-related organizations, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The law takes effect on July 1, today, and so we are not going to waste any time," DeSantis said.

HB 1471, officially titled "Systems of Law and Terrorist Organizations," authorizes Florida's Chief of Domestic Security to recommend designations for domestic or foreign terrorist groups. Those recommendations must then be approved or rejected by the governor and Florida Cabinet by majority vote before they take effect. Designated organizations can face public funding restrictions, possible corporate dissolution in certain circumstances, and penalties tied to material support. According to DeSantis, the designations would affect state and local funding, colleges and universities, and Florida's K-12 school choice scholarship program.

DeSantis presented Wednesday's announcement as a continuation and strengthening of a December executive order that targeted CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood. That earlier action was quickly challenged in federal court, and in March a judge temporarily blocked enforcement after CAIR, CAIR Florida, and civil rights groups sued, claiming it violated constitutional protections. DeSantis said the new law provides better legal footing for the state's efforts. "We did need to have more of a legal structure to be able to add teeth to these designations," he said. Glass echoed this sentiment, saying the law gives the state "more tools in the toolbox."

Attorneys representing CAIR signaled they expect another legal battle. Scott McCoy, deputy legal director of the Southern Poverty Law Center, stated that "regardless of what Gov. DeSantis calls it, the U.S. Constitution is supreme across our nation, including in Florida." He added that on CAIR's behalf, the Southern Poverty Law Center, American Civil Liberties Union, and other partners "look forward to responding in court." The designations remain unofficial until the Cabinet approves them. While no regular Cabinet meeting is scheduled for July, DeSantis indicated officials may convene in an emergency session to approve the designations.

cards.headline: DeSantis vetoes sovereign immunity bill that would have raised damage caps for first time in 16 years
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed legislation that would have modestly increased caps on damages payable in court settlements to people harmed by government negligence, ending a reform effort that passed with overwhelming bipartisan support.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed HB 145 on Wednesday, legislation that would have raised damage caps for government negligence claims for the first time in 16 years. The bill, sponsored by Sarasota Republican Rep. Fiona McFarland with a companion measure filed by Lake Mary Republican Sen. Jason Brodeur, would have increased caps from $200,000 per person and $300,000 per incident, last set in 2010, to $350,000 per person and $500,000 per incident. DeSantis said raising the caps would generate more unmeritorious lawsuits and that the current system effectively disincentivizes frivolous litigation. The measure passed with overwhelming bipartisan support in March.

The bill drew opposition from more than 240 registered lobbyists, including representatives from counties, cities and various agencies. It would have allowed local governments to voluntarily settle claims exceeding the caps without legislative approval and taken effect Oct. 1. McFarland argued the issue concerns equal protection under the law, noting that victims of government negligence face different compensation outcomes than those harmed by private entities. DeSantis countered that the current system works, noting he signed multiple claims bills this year providing people millions of dollars in compensation.

cards.headline: Attorney General sues TikTok over Florida social media law as most major platforms ignore compliance
cards.teaser: Attorney General James Uthmeier sued TikTok in June for violating Florida's social media law banning children under 14 from creating accounts. Most major tech companies covered under the law are not complying, with the notable exception of Meta.
cards.body:
After the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals cleared the way for Florida's HB 3 to take effect in November, Attorney General James Uthmeier moved aggressively to enforce the law, which bans children under 14 from creating social media accounts and requires parental consent for 14- and 15-year-olds. The legislation passed the Legislature in March 2024 and was signed that month by Governor Ron DeSantis. Despite threats of $50,000-per-violation fines that could compound into the billions, most major tech companies covered under the law are not complying. TikTok and Google, which owns YouTube and YouTube Kids, have effectively ignored the law and stayed silent on their compliance plans.

Meta announced it will comply with the law effective in early May and has suspended hundreds of thousands of accounts of underage kids. In June, Uthmeier sued TikTok, claiming it knowingly deceives parents and allows children to be exposed to harmful and inappropriate content in direct violation of Florida law. Google's silence is especially notable given YouTube's prominence in kids' online lives. Pew Research found roughly nine in 10 U.S. teens use YouTube, more than any other platform, with about three-quarters on it daily. Forty-six percent of parents whose children age 11 or younger use YouTube said their child had encountered inappropriate content on the platform. Uthmeier warned during a press conference that if holdouts don't follow Meta's lead, they will have to open their checkbook.

cards.headline: Florida Chamber poll finds 64% of state voters very proud to be American during 250th anniversary
cards.teaser: A statewide poll shows most Floridians are proud to be Americans during the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, though responses fall sharply along partisan and age lines.
cards.body:
A statewide poll conducted by the Florida Chamber of Commerce shows most Floridians are proud to be Americans during this 250th Anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. The poll found 64% of Floridians say they are "very proud" to be American, while another 12% say they are "somewhat proud" and 12% indicate they are not proud at all. Mark Wilson, President and CEO of the Florida Chamber of Commerce, said "Two hundred and fifty years ago the Founding Fathers set America on a course that has shaped the world ever since." The Chamber survey tapped 604 likely voters across the state between May 1 and May 9.

Perceptions of American pride fall along partisan lines. Some 89% of Republicans surveyed say they are very proud Americans, compared to about 34% of Democrats and 58% of no-party voters. About 25% of Democrats say they are not proud at all of being American, while only 2% of Republicans and 12% of no-party voters say the same. Responses also split significantly by age, with 71% of Floridians over 60 saying they are very proud to be American compared to just 42% under 40. On American history overall, 74% of Florida voters say Americans should be proud of the nation's history, while 12% say they feel ashamed. Republicans showed 91% support for pride in the nation's history compared to 51% of Democrats and 71% of no-party voters.

cards.headline: Saint Leo University and Town of St. Leo secure nearly $3 million in state budget
cards.teaser: Three budget projects survived Governor Ron DeSantis's veto pen, delivering funding to expand Saint Leo University's nursing program, build a cybersecurity training center, and support stormwater infrastructure for a proposed town center.
cards.body:
A trio of budget projects worth nearly $3 million survived Gov. Ron DeSantis' veto pen, delivering funding to Saint Leo University and the Town of St. Leo. Included in the $117.6 billion budget DeSantis signed this week, the allocations provide $1.2 million to expand the university's nursing program, $602,000 for its Cybersecurity and Cyberforensics Training and Education Center, and $995,000 for stormwater infrastructure supporting the Town of St. Leo's proposed town center. Zephyrhills Republican Sen. Danny Burgess and Dade City Republican Rep. Randy Maggard sponsored the budget requests.

The nursing funding addresses Florida's projected shortage of nearly 60,000 nurses by 2035, according to the Florida Hospital Association. Saint Leo's program has grown rapidly, jumping from 77 incoming pre-nursing students in Fall 2024 to 124 in Fall 2025, with enrollment expected to top 150 this fall. The project will reconfigure existing campus space to add three classrooms, a nursing lab, faculty offices, simulation equipment and classroom technology upgrades. The cybersecurity investment will fund construction of a Security Operations Center and cyberforensics laboratory, supporting hands-on training in digital defense, network monitoring and digital forensics while recruiting additional faculty. The town's $995,000 will support stormwater improvements for the proposed St. Leo Town Center, a mixed-use development featuring restaurants, retail, walking trails, a pavilion, botanical gardens and public gathering areas.

cards.headline: U.S. Sugar deploys autonomous tractors in largest commercial rollout in American sugar industry
cards.teaser: U.S. Sugar announced the largest commercial rollout of autonomous tractors in the American sugar industry, deploying five John Deere tractors that operate around the clock without a driver in the cab near Clewiston.
cards.body:
U.S. Sugar has deployed what it calls the largest commercial rollout of autonomous tractors in the American sugar industry. The company operates four John Deere 8R Series tractors and one 9R Series machine, each retrofitted to operate continuously without a driver. A single technician monitors multiple machines simultaneously from a remote command center. The autonomous technology comes from Autonomous Solutions, Inc., a Utah-based company that installs its Vehicle Automation Kit on the tractors' existing systems. Everglades Equipment Group supplied the tractors themselves.

The shift carries personal significance for workers like Harman Avalos, who previously drove tractors up to ten hours daily for three years. He now monitors those same machines from an air-conditioned trailer with a laptop. Precision Agriculture Manager Scott Berden notes that modern farming is far more high-tech than most people realize. U.S. Sugar plans to eventually expand the technology across its entire 250,000-acre operation, an area stretching about 375 miles and nearly ten times the size of Miami. Florida Trend's July issue traces the technology's backstory to Alberta, Canada, where ASI founder Mel Torrie spent his childhood missing school to drive tractors in circles for 16 hours a day, an experience that shaped his mission to autonomize the process.

cards.headline: Arizona Senator Mark Kelly endorses two Florida Democrats challenging Republican incumbents
cards.teaser: U.S. Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona endorsed Darren McAuley in his challenge to Rep. Gus Bilirakis and Bale Dalton in his race against Rep. Cory Mills, both citing the candidates' military backgrounds.
cards.body:
Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired Navy captain and former astronaut, endorsed two Florida Democrats challenging Republican incumbents. Kelly announced his support during a social media event backing 10 Democrats with military backgrounds running for Congress. "Veterans understand what it means to put country before self," Kelly posted. "These leaders did it during their time in service, and now they're answering the call again to fight for their communities in Congress." Kelly is married to gun safety activist Gabby Giffords, a former Congresswoman who survived an assassination attempt.

Bale Dalton is running in Florida's 7th Congressional District against GOP incumbent Cory Mills, a New Smyrna Republican. Dalton, recently named to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's Red to Blue program, served 24 years in the Navy and Navy Reserve and previously worked as Chief of Staff for NASA. "As a former Navy helicopter pilot and chief of staff at NASA, Bale Dalton knows the meaning of service," Kelly said. Darren McAuley is challenging 20-year incumbent Gus Bilirakis in Florida's 12th Congressional District. McAuley is a former Veterans Affairs physician and Florida's State Air Surgeon. Kelly said McAuley "is a physician and veteran who has spent his life helping others, including fellow service members and veterans."

hero.headline: Martin County free clinic sees surge in patients after enhanced ACA subsidies expire

cards.headline: One year after Alligator Alcatraz opened and closed, questions remain about billion-dollar facility
cards.teaser: The controversial immigration detention facility in the Everglades opened one year ago, then closed in June after costing Florida taxpayers an estimated $1 billion.
cards.body:
One year ago, Florida opened Alligator Alcatraz, a detention facility in the Everglades that became one of the most controversial immigration detention camps in the country. President Donald Trump announced the opening alongside Gov. Ron DeSantis on July 1, 2025. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County and built the facility in eight days using emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management. According to ICE's own data, about 70 percent of detainees had no criminal record, contradicting government claims that only dangerous migrants would be housed there. Immigration attorneys raised alarms about conditions inside. The American Civil Liberties Union filed a federal lawsuit over detainees' access to legal counsel, asserting attorneys could not show up without appointments and that clients were unable to place unmonitored outgoing calls to their lawyers.

The facility closed in June after detaining roughly 1,500 people at a time during its peak. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through Alligator Alcatraz. A $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers to cover costs estimated at more than $1 billion. ICE confirmed on June 16 that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. U.S. Rep. Maxwell Frost visited on May 26 and observed operations winding down. The ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits challenging the facility remain active.
